title: CBS Reported U.S. Preparations for Possible Renewed Strikes on Iran
description_short: On May 22, 2026, CBS reported preparations for possible renewed U.S. strikes on Iran while diplomacy continued; it said no final decision had been made.
description_medium: On May 22, 2026, CBS News reported that the Trump administration was preparing for possible renewed military strikes against Iran, citing sources with direct knowledge of planning. The report said diplomacy was continuing and no final decision had been made. Reuters separately reported Trump’s May 19 statement that the U.S. might strike again. These accounts describe consideration and preparation, not an order or completed strike.
description_long: On May 22, 2026, CBS News reported that the Trump administration was preparing for possible renewed military strikes against Iran while diplomatic talks continued. The report cited sources with direct knowledge of the planning and said no final decision to strike had been made. On May 19, Reuters reported that Trump said the United States might need to hit Iran again and had postponed a decision after coming close to ordering a strike. He said another attack could follow within days if no agreement was reached. The New York Times described possible target categories, including energy facilities, an underground nuclear-storage site at Isfahan and missile sites, if Trump chose to resume attacks. The reports concern separate dates, with Reuters covering Trump’s earlier public statement and CBS and the Times discussing later preparations and options. They describe planning and consideration, not a strike order or a completed attack on any listed site.
subcategory: Reported consideration of possible further strikes on Iran

title: DOJ Filed 31 Suits Seeking Unredacted Voter Registration Data
description_short: By October 1, 2026, DOJ had filed 31 voter-data suits against 30 states and Washington, D.C.; CBS reported that courts had rejected 26 cases.
description_medium: CBS News reported on October 1, 2026, that DOJ had filed 31 lawsuits against 30 states and Washington, D.C., seeking complete voter-registration lists. Some states had provided public versions but withheld unredacted files. CBS reported that federal judges had rejected 26 cases by then. A University of Wisconsin Law School tracker also describes the data sought as including sensitive identifiers.
description_long: As of October 1, 2026, CBS News reported that the Justice Department had filed 31 lawsuits against 30 states and Washington, D.C., seeking states’ complete voter-registration lists. The report said several states had provided publicly available versions of their voter rolls but declined to turn over the complete files. CBS counted 26 cases as rejected by federal judges by its publication date. The cases involved disputes over access to full registration records and requests for data beyond public versions. A University of Wisconsin Law School tracker also describes the requested information as sensitive, including driver’s-license and Social Security numbers. This is a dated snapshot of reported litigation and court rulings, not a final outcome for every case. The reports document the number of suits, states covered, requested records, and court actions available at that time; they do not say that all states withheld the same information or that every lawsuit had ended.

title: GAO Estimates $13.6 Million for Four Trump Mar-a-Lago Trips; $60,000 Paid to Resort
description_short: GAO estimated $13.6 million in federal costs for four 2017 Mar-a-Lago trips and identified about $60,000 in expenses paid to the resort.
description_medium: A 2019 GAO report estimated agencies incurred about $13.6 million for Trump’s four Mar-a-Lago trips from February 3 through March 5, 2017. It identified about $60,000 in expenses paid to Mar-a-Lago, including Defense Department lodging and Secret Service operational space. This is not a measure of total Trump Organization profit across all travel or properties.
description_long: The Government Accountability Office examined federal costs associated with four presidential trips to Mar-a-Lago between February 3 and March 5, 2017. GAO estimated that agencies incurred about $13.6 million for those trips, including approximately $10.6 million in government aircraft and boat operating costs and $3 million for temporary-duty expenses such as transportation, lodging, meals and incidentals. The estimate excluded certain classified information and salaries and benefits of personnel who would have been paid regardless of travel. GAO separately identified about $60,000 in expenses paid to Mar-a-Lago: roughly $24,000 for Defense Department lodging and $36,000 for Secret Service operational space. The report also found agencies had not consistently prepared required presidential-protection expenditure reports for Congress. The estimate covers four trips, not all presidential travel or all Trump properties, and it does not establish total Trump Organization profit across the presidency. The report thus provides a bounded cost estimate and a specific amount paid to the resort.

title: APHA Summarizes Project 2025 Proposals Affecting Public-Health Agencies
description_short: APHA says Project 2025 proposes limits on CDC guidance and changes to public-health agencies and federal civil-service protections.
description_medium: The American Public Health Association’s overview describes Project 2025 recommendations to limit CDC guidance on vaccines and masks, separate data collection from policy functions, and change civil-service protections. APHA warns that these proposals could affect public health and equity. Its page presents recommendations and potential effects, not evidence that the proposals became government rules.
description_long: The American Public Health Association’s overview describes Project 2025 as a set of recommendations for federal agencies. It says the plan would limit prescriptive CDC guidance on vaccines and masks, narrow some agency functions, and separate data collection from policy work. APHA also summarizes proposed changes to the FDA and NIH and a rollback of civil-service protections that could make federal employees easier to replace. The association warns that the proposals could harm public health and equity. These are descriptions of a policy plan and APHA’s assessment of possible effects. They do not establish that the proposals were implemented, or that the government imposed a general ban on scientists speaking publicly, monitored their publications, fired researchers for their speech, or removed whistleblower protections. The entry concerns Project 2025’s proposed changes to health agencies and the federal workforce, with the potential consequences attributed to APHA rather than stated as completed government action.
subcategory: Scientific Research Suppression and Researcher Persecution

preserved_fields.title: Government Scientists Gagging - Research Suppression and Whistleblower Persecution
preserved_fields.description_short: Government Scientists Gagging - Research Suppression and Whistleblower Persecution
preserved_fields.description_long: Donald Trump implemented systematic gagging of government scientists by prohibiting federal researchers from communicating their findings to the public while establishing surveillance and persecution systems that monitored scientific publications, conference presentations, and media communications to ensure compliance with administration ideology rather than scientific accuracy. The comprehensive scientist suppression represented elimination of federal researchers' ability to share objective findings about climate change, public health threats, environmental hazards, and other topics that conflicted with Trump's political agenda, creating what researchers called 'unprecedented assault on scientific integrity' that subordinated evidence-based research to ideological control. The systematic research suppression included requiring prior approval for all scientific communications, banning researchers from discussing climate change or environmental threats, and terminating scientists who shared findings that contradicted administration policies, effectively ending government's role in providing objective scientific information to protect public welfare. Trump's scientist gagging extended to eliminating whistleblower protections for federal researchers who exposed scientific misconduct, suppression of research findings, or manipulation of data for political purposes, creating systems where scientists faced termination, prosecution, or professional destruction for maintaining scientific integrity and ethical standards. The research persecution violated First Amendment protections for scientific speech while creating chilling effects that deterred government scientists from conducting objective research or sharing findings that served public interest rather than political agenda, transforming federal scientific agencies from sources of evidence-based information into propaganda operations. The scientific suppression represented what researchers called completion of 'war on science' that eliminated government's capacity to provide accurate information about threats to public health, environmental safety, and national security, prioritizing ideological conformity over scientific evidence that had historically informed policy decisions and protected American lives.

title: Steven Levitsky Described U.S. Democracy Under Trump as Competitive Authoritarianism
description_short: In April 2025, Steven Levitsky told NPR the U.S. had crossed into “competitive authoritarianism”; this is his assessment, not proof that constitutional government ended.
description_medium: In an April 22, 2025 NPR interview, Harvard political scientist Steven Levitsky said the United States was “no longer living in a democratic regime” and described it as having crossed into competitive authoritarianism. He cited threats and attacks against critics and institutions during Trump’s first months back in office. These were Levitsky’s assessment and examples, not a formal finding that every democratic check had ended.
description_long: On April 22, 2025, NPR’s Fresh Air interviewed Harvard political scientist Steven Levitsky about democracy under President Donald Trump. Levitsky said he was pessimistic in the short term and stated that the United States was “no longer living in a democratic regime,” describing it as having crossed into “competitive authoritarianism.” He pointed to what he characterized as government weaponization and threats or attacks involving law firms, company leaders, media, universities, nongovernmental organizations, and critics during Trump’s first four months back in office. These statements are Levitsky’s analysis, as reported in the interview. The interview documents his assessment and examples; it does not establish that constitutional government formally ended, that every democratic check was eliminated, or that the United States became a permanent autocracy. His comments described what he saw as rapid democratic backsliding early in the administration. He offered that assessment in an interview about democracy under Trump.

preserved_fields.description_short: American Democratic Republic Final Collapse - 248 Years of Constitutional Government Terminated
preserved_fields.description_long: Donald Trump completed the final collapse of American constitutional democracy by systematically eliminating all remaining democratic institutions, constitutional protections, and rule of law while establishing permanent authoritarian control through Project 2025's comprehensive transformation of the United States from a federal republic into a personalized autocracy controlled by Trump and his loyalist network. The democratic republic's final destruction represented culmination of systematic institutional capture that eliminated judicial independence through loyalist court control, legislative authority through executive power concentration, federal agency independence through Schedule F reclassification, state autonomy through funding coercion, civil society through surveillance and persecution, media independence through access control, and constitutional rights through systematic violation and elimination. Trump's republic termination violated every foundational principle of American governance by concentrating all governmental power under personal control while using state authority for self-enrichment, political persecution, ideological enforcement, and authoritarian control rather than constitutional obligations to protect rights, serve the public, and maintain democratic processes that had defined American government for 248 years. The systematic democracy elimination created what international observers recognized as competitive authoritarianism where electoral forms remained but were rendered meaningless through surveillance, persecution, media control, legal system capture, and systematic intimidation that prevented meaningful political competition, peaceful transfer of power, or constitutional governance. The American Republic's final destruction represented implementation of Project 2025's explicit goal to create 'imperial presidency' that eliminated all constitutional constraints while establishing personalized rule based on loyalty to Trump rather than constitutional principles, democratic norms, rule of law, or institutional accountability that had maintained American democracy since 1776. The constitutional democracy termination transformed the United States from the world's oldest constitutional republic into an authoritarian state controlled by Trump through personal networks, loyalty tests, systematic persecution of opponents, and complete elimination of democratic constraints, completing the most comprehensive destruction of democratic governance in world history.

title: Bukele Offers to House U.S. Deportees in Salvadoran Prisons
description_short: In February 2025, El Salvador offered to house U.S. deportees, including convicted citizens; the offer did not establish a completed deal or transfer.
description_medium: Reuters reported that Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele offered to accept deportees from the United States and house them in Salvadoran prisons. The reports describe an offer and discussions, not a completed arrangement to deport Americans to CECOT. They do not identify a signed agreement, transfer authority, or an American sent there.
description_long: In February 2025, after meeting Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele offered to accept people deported from the United States and house them in Salvadoran prisons. Rubio described the offer as covering dangerous criminals of any nationality. Bukele later said it included convicted U.S. citizens, in exchange for a fee. Reuters reported the offer but did not describe a signed agreement or an implemented transfer of American citizens. The proposal was discussed amid the Trump administration’s deportation campaign, but a foreign leader’s offer did not itself authorize the United States to send citizens abroad. The Associated Press also reported Rubio’s description of the offer’s possible scope. The public statements left the precise terms and legal mechanism unsettled. The sources document an offer and discussion, not a completed arrangement, U.S. legal authorization, or evidence that an American was sent to CECOT or another Salvadoran prison.

title: Colorado Lawsuit Cites White House Email on Federal Actions Toward the State
description_short: Colorado attorneys cited a December 2025 White House email inviting agencies to discuss immediate actions concerning the state.
description_medium: CBS Colorado reported that Colorado attorneys cited a December 15, 2025 email from White House staffer Emily Underwood in a lawsuit alleging retaliation over election policy and the prosecution of Tina Peters. The message invited officials from several agencies to discuss “immediate actions” concerning Colorado. The White House disputed a connection to Peters, so the email is evidence cited by plaintiffs, not a judicial finding of retaliation.
description_long: News reports describe a December 15, 2025 email from White House staffer Emily Underwood inviting officials at five federal agencies to discuss “immediate actions” concerning Colorado. The message reportedly said the goal was to prioritize the state so grants and federal support aligned with administration priorities.
